newsitem.title: LEBANON: World Bank backs Hariri, boosts aid for Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: World Bank backs Hariri, boosts aid for Lebanon.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn announced a big increase in funding for Lebanon and declared his backing for Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's much criticised deficit financing of national reconstruction.

On his first visit to Beirut, Wolfensohn went out of his way at a late-night news conference on Sunday to express confidence in Hariri's policy of accumulating debt to finance rapid reconstruction which some Lebanese politicians, bankers and economists have criticised.
Wolfensohn said he would do the same thing as Hariri if he were in his shoes.
"We very much trust the government and believe in what they are doing," he said, announcing that the bank had quadrupled funding for Lebanon to $400 million a year from $100 million.

The World Bank and its private sector arm the International Finance Corporation (IFC) had allocated a total $420 million to Lebanon in 1997, Wolfensohn said. The bank also increased emergency funding by $50 million to a total of $150 million.
The additional aid follows a pledge Wolfensohn made during Israel's 17-day blitz of Lebanon in April 1996 to put in place a solid programme of financial assistance for Lebanon.
"There is literally no holdback on the part of the bank. There are no conditions to be met," he said of the new basket of aid.

Wolfensohn said the bank had already approved programmes for Lebanon totalling $600 million. Another $1 billion pledged at a donors conference in Washington in December would be approved and the IFC was providing $150 million a year.

These amounts were "very, very, high" in comparison with the bank's contribution to other Middle Eastern countries and he expected spending of the money by Lebanon to speed up now after a slow beginning.
Hariri said World Bank and IFC contributions would total $2.2 billion over the next four years.
Asked about Lebanon's massive budget deficits and ballooning public debt, Wolfensohn said he was concerned about the debt but he trusted the "financial good sense" of Hariri's government.

"It seems to me that when you're trying to do a lot very quickly after a conflict you either have a choice of meeting peacetime standards or possibly taking risks in order to get things moving," he said.
"If I were in the shoes of the prime minister I would try and move quickly but have the diligence I know that he and the finance minister (Fouad Siniora) bring to it."

Francois Bassil, president of the Lebanese Banks' Association, warned last week that the deficits and debt were endangering everything Hariri had achieved since October 1993 in rebuilding Lebanon from the ruins of the 1975-90 civil war.
Total debt has risen since end 1993 to 17.5 trillion Lebanese pounds ($11.4 billion) from five trillion. This is nearly 83 percent of estimated GDP of $13.9 billion at end 1996.
This year's deficit of government income against expenditure was 60.2 percent at end May compared with a 36 percent annual target set in the budget law.
"Of course we are concerned about the high levels of debt but I am sure the government is more concerned than we are, so I'm prepared to leave it in their hands to worry about," Wolfensohn said.
"Until proven otherwise, it's my judgment that you can trust the financial good sense of this administration," he added.
